about.headline: From pixels to pipelines.
about.headline_sub: 20 years of building things that work.
about.body: I started by obsessing over single pixels in a photography studio — lighting, composition, the science of making products sell. That obsession with precision led me through marketing at industrial plants, into web development, and finally into AI architecture. The AI here is all Google’s own — a Gemma 4 I fine-tuned and self-host, EmbeddingGemma for search, Chirp 3 for voice.
about.body2: My engineering philosophy was forged by necessity. I build systems designed to run autonomously, scale without me, and fail gracefully. Every architecture decision asks one question: "Will this still work when I can't be there?"

embeddings.clusterSilhouetteTooltip: Mean silhouette score across all points, from -1 to 1 — higher means the discovered groups are more cleanly separated.
embeddings.exactScoreNote: Scores below are exact cosine similarity, computed in full embedding space — the 3D positions above are a lossy, dimensionality-reduced layout.

embeddings.layoutPcaTooltip: PCA projects the whole point cloud in one fast linear pass — an instant approximate layout, computed synchronously on the main thread.
embeddings.layoutUmapTooltip: UMAP iteratively optimizes a layout that preserves local neighborhoods more faithfully than PCA — slower, so it runs in a background Web Worker.
embeddings.refiningLayoutTooltip: The same approximate-now, exact-later trade-off RAG systems make: an instant PCA layout renders first, then a slower, more accurate UMAP layout swaps in once it's ready.

embeddings.chunkingIntro: How a document gets cut into chunks before embedding directly shapes what a RAG pipeline can retrieve later. Too coarse and one relevant sentence drowns in unrelated text; too fine and a chunk loses the context it needs to make sense on its own. Try each strategy on the same document below.
embeddings.chunkingSampleText:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation grounds a language model's answers in an external corpus instead of relying purely on facts memorized during training. A typical RAG pipeline has three stages: chunking the source documents, embedding each chunk into a vector, and retrieving the closest chunks to a user's query at answer time.

How a document gets cut into chunks has an outsized effect on retrieval quality. Chunks that are too large dilute a passage's semantic focus, burying the one relevant sentence inside paragraphs of unrelated text and pulling its embedding toward some watered-down average meaning. Chunks that are too small lose the surrounding context a reader — or a language model — needs to make sense of a fact, an example, or a pronoun's antecedent.

Fixed-size chunking is the simplest strategy: cut the text every N characters, optionally overlapping consecutive chunks so a sentence that straddles a boundary still survives intact somewhere. Sentence-based chunking respects punctuation instead of raw character counts, so no chunk ends mid-thought. Semantic chunking goes a step further and embeds each sentence, starting a new chunk only when the topic actually shifts — the closest thing to how a human would section the same document by hand.

Web engineers building a RAG pipeline face an extra constraint: the embedding model itself has to run somewhere. This demo sends every embedding call over the network to a self-hosted EmbeddingGemma running on the studio's own inference server, instead of downloading a model into the browser — the trade-off shifts from client compute to a network round trip and the server's own capacity to keep up.
embeddings.chunkingEmbeddingStatus: Embedding sentences to detect topic shifts…
embeddings.chunkingError: Chunking failed — try a shorter document or a different strategy.
embeddings.chunkingSemanticTruncatedNotice: Showing the first {n} sentences — the document was truncated for this semantic-chunking demo.
embeddings.chunkingExplainerFixed: Fixed windows are cheap, predictable, and model-free — but they cut mid-sentence and mid-idea with no regard for meaning. Overlap patches over lost context at the boundary, at the cost of duplicating that text across two chunks in the index.
embeddings.chunkingExplainerSentence: Sentence boundaries keep every chunk a complete, punctuation-respecting thought. But a single short sentence can be too little context on its own, and this strategy still can't tell where one topic ends and the next begins.
embeddings.chunkingExplainerSemantic: Embedding each sentence and cutting where adjacent similarity drops tracks where the topic actually shifts — the most retrieval-friendly boundary, since each chunk stays about one thing. The cost is one embedding call per sentence before you even index the document.
embeddings.chunkingLateChunkingNote: Not demonstrated here: late chunking and multi-vector retrieval (ColBERT-style). Both need per-token embeddings before pooling — the server's /api/embed endpoint only returns already-pooled sentence vectors.
embeddings.retrievalIntro: The same query, retrieved three different ways over the same embedded corpus. Dense search alone can miss exact keywords a paraphrase blurs past; hybrid search blends in lexical (BM25) matching to catch them; reranking then reorders a wider candidate pool for relevance and diversity together. Watch the rank badges — they show exactly what each step changed.
embeddings.retrievalQueryPlaceholder: Try a query mixing an exact term with a paraphrase…
embeddings.retrievalAlphaDisabledNote: RRF has no α — it fuses purely by rank position, not by how much one score beat another.
embeddings.retrievalHybridScaleNote: Hybrid's score is a normalized dense+lexical blend on its own scale — not directly comparable to the raw cosine scores in the other columns.
embeddings.retrievalRrfScoreNote: RRF scores are cumulative reciprocal ranks (Σ 1/(k+rank)) — small numbers by design, and not comparable to the min-max scale or to a different-sized result set.
embeddings.retrievalEmptyPlaceholder: Type a query above to compare retrieval strategies.
embeddings.retrievalExplainerHybrid: Hybrid search min-max normalizes dense cosine similarity and BM25 lexical scores, then blends them as α·dense + (1−α)·lexical. Raising α trusts meaning over wording; lowering it favors exact keyword/acronym matches a paraphrase-blind dense model can miss.
embeddings.retrievalExplainerRrf: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) ignores raw score magnitude entirely and fuses by RANK: each result's fused score is Σ 1/(k+rank) across the dense and lexical rankings (k=60, the standard default). That makes it immune to one signal's score scale dominating the blend — min-max blending's real failure mode when cosine similarities and BM25 scores have wildly different spreads — which is why RRF is the boring-but-safe 2026 default in production hybrid search (Elastic, Qdrant, OpenSearch). The cost: it can't tell a landslide win from a narrow one, only that one result outranked another. One honest caveat about this demo specifically: textbook RRF fuses truncated top-K lists from separate search engines — here both retrievers instead rank the whole demo corpus before fusion, since it's small enough to score exhaustively.
embeddings.retrievalExplainerRerank: MMR reranking takes the top dense candidates and greedily reorders them to maximize λ·relevance − (1−λ)·similarity-to-already-picked. Lower λ trades some relevance for diversity, so near-duplicate top hits don't crowd out a distinct, still-relevant passage.
embeddings.retrievalCandidatePoolNote: Reranking draws its candidates from the top {n} dense results.
embeddings.retrievalLlmExperimentalNote: Experimental — LLM-as-judge via the self-hosted Gemma model, one listwise call per run.
embeddings.retrievalLlmUnavailable: Needs the live inference server — the backend is unreachable, so no relevance judgment ran.
embeddings.retrievalLlmParseError: The judge model returned an unparseable ranking — a real failure mode of small LLMs asked for strict JSON.
embeddings.retrievalLlmNotScored: Not scored by the judge — dropped from its reply, not ranked last

prompt.outputHint: Output cost depends on how long the model's reply is, which can't be known in advance — pick an expected length so the estimate matches your use case.

prompt.overheadTierEstimatedTooltip: Estimated — this provider's exact wrapper tokens can't be measured client-side (Anthropic/Google's API, or a self-hosted model's real per-conversation template). Treat as an order-of-magnitude placeholder, not an exact count.
prompt.cacheBelowFloorHint: Below the {min}-token minimum cacheable prefix — the provider would not cache this, so it's billed as fresh input on every call.
prompt.cacheBelowFloorSummary: {tokens} tokens are marked cacheable but sit below this model's {min}-token minimum — the provider won't actually cache them; they're billed as fresh input above instead.
prompt.cacheBreakpointWarning: {count} cacheable blocks exceed Anthropic's documented limit of 4 cache breakpoints per request — only the first 4 would actually be cached.
prompt.cacheExportNoteAnthropic: The Anthropic Messages API export below includes real cache_control markers on the first 4 cacheable blocks — these savings are realizable exactly as exported.
prompt.cacheExportNoteAutomatic: This provider caches repeated prefixes automatically server-side — no export markers are needed for the savings above to apply.
prompt.exportAnthropicRoleWarning: This export would start with an assistant turn and there's no context block to promote into a leading user turn — Anthropic's Messages API requires the first message to be user. Add a leading user block before sending this payload.
prompt.hiddenReasoningNotice: This model may generate hidden reasoning tokens billed as output but never shown in the response — actual output cost can be several times the estimate above. This tool can't count them; they're decided at generation time.
